messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Thom

Thom was sixty-eight when the bomb went off outside the community centre in Kuala Lumpur where he was coordinating resettlement paperwork for a group of Rohingya families. The blast came without warning—a concussive roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once, followed by the sound of glass cascading onto concrete and the screams of people he had been speaking with moments before. He remembered the heat on his face, the acrid smell of smoke, the way the fluorescent lights flickered and died. What he could not quite reconcile, even now four years later, was that it had happened at all. When he tried to reconstruct those minutes, the images felt almost cinematic—too vivid, too perfectly terrible to be real. He would see the face of Amara, one of the case workers, frozen in an expression of confusion just before the windows exploded inward. He would see the papers on his desk scattered like snow. But the memory had a dreamlike quality that made him doubt himself, as though his mind was playing a trick, exaggerating what had actually occurred. The auditory fragments were worse: at unpredictable moments, he would hear the initial whistle of the blast, the high-pitched ringing that had filled his ears in those first seconds, sounds that seemed to play from inside his own skull rather than from any external source.

It was this very unreality of the memories—the way they felt both hyperreal and impossible—that had driven Thom into a pattern of rumination from which he could not escape. He would lie awake at night replaying the sequence, trying to convince himself that it had truly happened, and in doing so, would inevitably spiral into self-blame. Why had he been at his desk that morning? He could have been in the back office. Why had he not noticed something amiss in the minutes before? Other aid workers had survived similar incidents by sensing danger; he had sensed nothing. He had been negligent, inattentive, and in his negligence, people had died. Amara had two young children. This thought would return to him dozens of times a day, each recurrence accompanied by a fresh wave of guilt. He had come to believe that if he could just understand what he had done wrong, if he could fully accept his culpability, then perhaps the memories would finally make sense—would solidify into something he could live with rather than something that haunted him like a ghost that refused to take solid form.

The intrusive images and sounds had also fundamentally altered how Thom perceived the world as dangerous. In the weeks following the blast, he had noticed that ordinary noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the sharp crack of a wooden spoon against a pot in his kitchen—would send him into a state of acute alarm, his body tensing as though another explosion were imminent. His wife, Mei, had learned not to move suddenly around him. More insidiously, the sense of threat had begun to contract the geography of his life. He no longer felt safe driving or riding in cars; the enclosed space, the sense of exposure on the roads, the unpredictability of other vehicles—all of it felt like a trap waiting to spring. He had stopped taking the bus to the office. Within a year, he had effectively confined himself to his home and the homes of a handful of trusted friends, places where he could control the environment and the exits. His work as a refugee aid worker, the career that had given his life meaning for thirty-seven years, had become impossible. He had taken early retirement at sixty-nine, telling his supervisor that his health was failing, which was not entirely untrue.

The contraction of his world and the hypervigilance that accompanied it only deepened his rumination. Trapped in his safe zones, with hours stretching before him, Thom found himself returning obsessively to the question of what he should have done differently. He had begun avoiding any conversation with Mei that might lead to disagreement or conflict, fearing that confrontation would destabilize him further, that any emotional turbulence might trigger the memories more intensely. She had gently suggested that he see a therapist, and he had refused for two years, convinced that talking about it would only make the memories feel more real, more undeniable. But last month, after a particularly bad night in which the auditory flashbacks had been so vivid that he had called out in his sleep, Mei had insisted. Now, at seventy-two, Thom sits in a therapist's office for the first time, exhausted by the weight of memories that feel simultaneously impossible and utterly consuming, desperate to understand whether he can ever forgive himself for something he cannot quite believe he survived.

violation_explanations: The vignette describes both intrusive memory and threat perception, but does not establish a causal relationship between them; the memory's unreality drives rumination, and threat perception is described as a separate consequence of the blast, but no paragraph conveys that the memory itself drives or influences the sense of threat.
